claim: Robo2 is broadly expressed in the adult brain with the highest expression in the ventral midbrain, hippocampus and cerebellum.
source: Analysis of the Allen Institute mouse brain expression atlas (Lein et al., 2007) reveals that Robo2 is broadly expressed in the adult brain with the highest expression in the ventral midbrain, hippocampus and cerebellum, similar to previous reports (Marillat et al., 2002) (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Supported by in situ hybridization data from the Allen Institute mouse brain expression atlas and reference to previous reports (Marillat et al., 2002).

claim: Robo2 expression was observed throughout the VTA, largely localized to TH-positive neurons.
source: Robo2 expression was observed throughout the VTA, largely localized to TH-positive neurons, though several TH-negative neurons were observed to also express Robo2 (TH+Robo2+ = 75.28 ± 0.56%, TH+Robo2− = 7.81 ± 1.46%, and TH-Robo2+ = 16.90 ± 1.77%, n = 4) (Figure 1A).
evidence: Supported by immunostaining data showing quantification of Robo2 and TH co-expression in VTA neurons.

claim: 75.28% of VTA cells are TH-positive and Robo2-positive.
source: Robo2 expression was observed throughout the VTA, largely localized to TH-positive neurons, though several TH-negative neurons were observed to also express Robo2 (TH+Robo2+ = 75.28 ± 0.56%, TH+Robo2− = 7.81 ± 1.46%, and TH-Robo2+ = 16.90 ± 1.77%, n = 4) (Figure 1A).
evidence: Supported by quantitative immunostaining data from VTA sections.

claim: Robo2 mRNA is enriched in both midbrain dopamine and midbrain GABA neurons.
source: We found Robo2 to have enriched expression in the IP fraction relative to the input in both mouse lines (Figure 1—figure supplement 1F) confirming Robo2 expression in both dopamine and GABA neurons of the midbrain neurons.
evidence: Supported by Ribotag immunoprecipitation and qRT-PCR data from Slc6a3Cre and Slc32a1Cre mouse lines.

claim: Following Robo2 inactivation in the adult VTA, sIPSC frequency is reduced in Ih-positive neurons.
source: In contrast, we did observe a significant reduction in sIPSC frequency in mutant mice relative to controls (Figure 1D–E), with no change in sIPSC amplitude (Figure 1D and F).
evidence: Supported by whole-cell patch-clamp recordings from Ih-positive neurons in acute brain slices.

claim: Following Robo2 inactivation in the adult VTA, sIPSC amplitude is not altered in Ih-positive neurons.
source: In contrast, we did observe a significant reduction in sIPSC frequency in mutant mice relative to controls (Figure 1D–E), with no change in sIPSC amplitude (Figure 1D and F).
evidence: Supported by whole-cell patch-clamp recordings from Ih-positive neurons in acute brain slices.

claim: Following Robo2 inactivation in the adult VTA, sEPSC frequency is not altered in Ih-positive neurons.
source: Surprisingly, we did not observe significant changes in either sEPSC frequency or amplitude (Figure 1—figure supplement 2B-DA-C).
evidence: Supported by whole-cell patch-clamp recordings from Ih-positive neurons in acute brain slices.

claim: Following Robo2 inactivation in the adult VTA, sEPSC amplitude is not altered in Ih-positive neurons.
source: Surprisingly, we did not observe significant changes in either sEPSC frequency or amplitude (Figure 1—figure supplement 2B-DA-C).
evidence: Supported by whole-cell patch-clamp recordings from Ih-positive neurons in acute brain slices.

claim: Following Robo2 inactivation in the adult VTA, sIPSC frequency is reduced in Ih-negative neurons.
source: Similar to putative dopamine neurons, sIPSC frequency was reduced in Ih-negative neurons and sIPSC amplitude was not altered (Figure 1G–I).
evidence: Supported by whole-cell patch-clamp recordings from Ih-negative neurons in acute brain slices.

claim: Following Robo2 inactivation in the adult VTA, sIPSC amplitude is not altered in Ih-negative neurons.
source: Similar to putative dopamine neurons, sIPSC frequency was reduced in Ih-negative neurons and sIPSC amplitude was not altered (Figure 1G–I).
evidence: Supported by whole-cell patch-clamp recordings from Ih-negative neurons in acute brain slices.

claim: Following Robo2 inactivation in the adult VTA, sEPSC frequency is not altered in Ih-negative neurons.
source: We also did not observe differences in sEPSCs in these neurons (Figure 1—figure supplement 2F-HD-F).
evidence: Supported by whole-cell patch-clamp recordings from Ih-negative neurons in acute brain slices.

claim: Ultrastructural analysis of synaptic contacts did not reveal gross morphological differences in either symmetrical or asymmetrical synapses following Robo2 inactivation.
source: Ultrastructural analysis of synaptic contacts using transmission electron microscopy did not reveal gross morphological differences in either symmetrical (inhibitory) or asymmetrical (excitatory) synapses (Figure 1—figure supplement 3A), nor the number of observable synapses (Figure 1—figure supplement 3B)
evidence: Supported by transmission electron microscopy analysis of VTA synapses.

claim: The number of observable synapses is not altered following Robo2 inactivation in the adult VTA.
source: Ultrastructural analysis of synaptic contacts using transmission electron microscopy did not reveal gross morphological differences in either symmetrical (inhibitory) or asymmetrical (excitatory) synapses (Figure 1—figure supplement 3A), nor the number of observable synapses (Figure 1—figure supplement 3B)
evidence: Supported by transmission electron microscopy analysis of VTA synapses.

claim: The inactivation kinetics of sIPSCs are not altered following Robo2 inactivation, suggesting that the subunit composition of the postsynaptic GABAA receptors is not altered.
source: Additionally, we did not observe differences in the inactivation kinetics of sIPSCs suggesting that the subunit composition of the postsynaptic GABAA receptors is not altered (Figure 1—figure supplement 3C–F).
evidence: Supported by analysis of sIPSC decay kinetics from patch-clamp recordings.

claim: Following Robo2 inactivation in the adult VTA, there is no difference in the basal firing rate of putative dopamine neurons.
source: We observed no difference between controls and Robo2 VTA mutants in the basal firing rate (Figure 2C), nor did we detect significant differences in the number of burst firing, or phasic events (Figure 2D).
evidence: Supported by in vivo single-unit electrophysiology recordings from VTA neurons.

claim: Following Robo2 inactivation in the adult VTA, there is no significant difference in the number of burst firing events in putative dopamine neurons.
source: We observed no difference between controls and Robo2 VTA mutants in the basal firing rate (Figure 2C), nor did we detect significant differences in the number of burst firing, or phasic events (Figure 2D).
evidence: Supported by in vivo single-unit electrophysiology recordings from VTA neurons.

claim: Following Robo2 inactivation in the adult VTA, there is a significant increase in the duration of burst events in putative dopamine neurons.
source: In contrast, we did observe a significant increase in the duration of burst events (Figure 2E) and the number of spikes per burst (Figure 2F), consistent with a reduced inhibitory termination of burst epochs.
evidence: Supported by in vivo single-unit electrophysiology recordings from VTA neurons.

claim: Following Robo2 inactivation in the adult VTA, there is a significant increase in the number of spikes per burst in putative dopamine neurons.
source: In contrast, we did observe a significant increase in the duration of burst events (Figure 2E) and the number of spikes per burst (Figure 2F), consistent with a reduced inhibitory termination of burst epochs.
evidence: Supported by in vivo single-unit electrophysiology recordings from VTA neurons.

claim: The increased burst duration and spikes per burst in putative dopamine neurons following Robo2 inactivation is consistent with a reduced inhibitory termination of burst epochs.
source: In contrast, we did observe a significant increase in the duration of burst events (Figure 2E) and the number of spikes per burst (Figure 2F), consistent with a reduced inhibitory termination of burst epochs.
evidence: Inference based on the observed increase in burst duration and spikes per burst.

claim: Following Robo2 inactivation in the adult VTA, there is no difference in the firing rate of putative non-dopamine neurons.
source: Similar to putative dopamine neurons, quinpirole insensitive neurons did not show changes in overall firing rate (Figure 2G).
evidence: Supported by in vivo single-unit electrophysiology recordings from VTA neurons.

claim: Following Robo2 inactivation in the adult VTA, putative non-dopamine neurons show a significant change in the skew of their interspike-interval distribution.
source: However, these cells did show a significant change in the skew of their interspike-interval distribution (ISI, Figure 2H–I).
evidence: Supported by in vivo single-unit electrophysiology recordings from VTA neurons.

claim: Following Robo2 inactivation in the adult VTA, putative non-dopamine neurons show a reduction in the coefficient of variation of the ISI.
source: Consistent with this change in ISI distribution, quinpirole insensitive neurons showed a reduction in the coefficient of variation of the ISI (CV-ISI, Figure 2J), indicative of a reduced number of inhibitory pauses.
evidence: Supported by in vivo single-unit electrophysiology recordings from VTA neurons.

claim: The reduction in CV-ISI in putative non-dopamine neurons following Robo2 inactivation is indicative of a reduced number of inhibitory pauses.
source: Consistent with this change in ISI distribution, quinpirole insensitive neurons showed a reduction in the coefficient of variation of the ISI (CV-ISI, Figure 2J), indicative of a reduced number of inhibitory pauses.
evidence: Inference based on the observed reduction in CV-ISI.

claim: At lower stimulus intensities, dopamine release in the nucleus accumbens is significantly elevated in Robo2 mutant mice compared to controls following PPTg stimulation.
source: At lower stimulus intensities, dopamine release was significantly elevated in Robo2 mutant mice compared to controls (Figure 3C–H).
evidence: Supported by fast scan cyclic voltammetry measurements of dopamine release in the nucleus accumbens.

claim: There are no significant differences in dopamine release evoked by direct stimulation of the medial forebrain bundle following Robo2 inactivation.
source: We did not observe significant differences in dopamine release evoked by direct stimulation of the medial forebrain bundle (MFB; Figure 3—figure supplement 1E–J), suggesting that dopamine transporter function is not altered in Robo2 mutant mice.
evidence: Supported by fast scan cyclic voltammetry measurements of dopamine release following MFB stimulation.

claim: Dopamine transporter function is not altered in Robo2 mutant mice.
source: We did not observe significant differences in dopamine release evoked by direct stimulation of the medial forebrain bundle (MFB; Figure 3—figure supplement 1E–J), suggesting that dopamine transporter function is not altered in Robo2 mutant mice.
evidence: Inference based on the lack of differences in dopamine release following MFB stimulation.

claim: Tonic dopamine release is not altered in Robo2 mutant mice as measured by microdialysis.
source: Consistent with a lack of observed differences in the overall firing rate of dopamine neurons (Figure 2C), we did not detect differences in tonic dopamine release as measured by microdialysis (Figure 3—figure supplement 1K–L).
evidence: Supported by microdialysis-UPLC measurements of tonic dopamine levels in the nucleus accumbens.

claim: Robo2 mutant mice are significantly hyperactive compared to controls, particularly during the night.
source: Robo2 mutants were significantly hyperactive compared to controls (Figure 4A), particularly during the night (Figure 4B).
evidence: Supported by locomotor activity measurements across the day-night cycle.

claim: Robo2 mutant mice show reduced forelimb separation and greater print separation compared to controls.
source: Consistent with altered locomotion in mutant mice, we observed reduced forelimb separation and greater print separation (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A–F).
evidence: Supported by footprint analysis data.

claim: Control mice show a characteristic locomotor sensitization to cocaine.
source: In control mice, we observed a characteristic locomotor sensitization to cocaine (Figure 4C–E).
evidence: Supported by locomotor activity measurements following daily cocaine injections.

claim: Robo2 mutant mice show an inversion in the normal locomotor response to cocaine, decreasing rather than increasing their activity.
source: In contrast, Robo2 mutant mice showed an inversion in the normal locomotor response to cocaine (Figure 4C–E), decreasing rather than increasing their activity; this pattern persisted across days.
evidence: Supported by locomotor activity measurements following daily cocaine injections.

claim: The inverted psychomotor response to cocaine in Robo2 mutant mice persists across days.
source: In contrast, Robo2 mutant mice showed an inversion in the normal locomotor response to cocaine (Figure 4C–E), decreasing rather than increasing their activity; this pattern persisted across days.
evidence: Supported by locomotor activity measurements following daily cocaine injections over 5 days.

claim: Cocaine CPP is not as robust in Robo2 mutant mice compared to controls, but it does not lead to an avoidance of the cocaine-paired side.
source: Although cocaine CPP was not as robust in mutant mice compared to controls (Figure 4—figure supplement 2A), it did not lead to an avoidance of the cocaine-paired side, suggesting that although their psychomotor response is altered, the hedonic aspect of cocaine is not significantly changed.
evidence: Supported by conditioned place preference measurements.

claim: The hedonic aspect of cocaine is not significantly changed in Robo2 mutant mice.
source: Although cocaine CPP was not as robust in mutant mice compared to controls (Figure 4—figure supplement 2A), it did not lead to an avoidance of the cocaine-paired side, suggesting that although their psychomotor response is altered, the hedonic aspect of cocaine is not significantly changed.
evidence: Inference based on the lack of avoidance of the cocaine-paired side in CPP.

claim: Robo2 mutant mice have inverted locomotor responses to amphetamine.
source: Similar to their response to cocaine, Robo2 mutant mice had inverted locomotor responses to amphetamine (AMP) and the DAT blocker GBR12909 (GBR; Figure 4F–H).
evidence: Supported by locomotor activity measurements following amphetamine injection.

claim: Robo2 mutant mice have inverted locomotor responses to the DAT blocker GBR12909.
source: Similar to their response to cocaine, Robo2 mutant mice had inverted locomotor responses to amphetamine (AMP) and the DAT blocker GBR12909 (GBR; Figure 4F–H).
evidence: Supported by locomotor activity measurements following GBR12909 injection.

claim: Robo2 mutant mice show greater inhibition in response to the serotonin transport blocker fluoxetine compared to controls.
source: Robo2 mutant mice also had a differential response to the serotonin transport blocker fluoxetine with the mutants showing greater inhibition, but the norepinephrine transport blocker nisoxetine reduced activity equally in control and mutant mice (Figure 4—figure supplement 2B–E).
evidence: Supported by locomotor activity measurements following fluoxetine injection.

claim: The norepinephrine transport blocker nisoxetine reduces activity equally in control and Robo2 mutant mice.
source: Robo2 mutant mice also had a differential response to the serotonin transport blocker fluoxetine with the mutants showing greater inhibition, but the norepinephrine transport blocker nisoxetine reduced activity equally in control and mutant mice (Figure 4—figure supplement 2B–E).
evidence: Supported by locomotor activity measurements following nisoxetine injection.

claim: Robo2 mutant mice show significant deficits in Pavlovian associative learning, failing to discriminate between predictive and non-predictive cues.
source: Robo2 mutant mice showed significant deficits in this task compared to control mice, with mutant mice failing to discriminate between predictive (CSplus) and non-predictive (CSminus) cues (Figure 4I).
evidence: Supported by Pavlovian conditioning behavioral data.

claim: The learning impairment in Robo2 mutant mice is not associated with a reduction in reward seeking.
source: This impairment was not associated with a reduction in reward seeking as total head entries into the reward receptacle did not differ (Figure 4—figure supplement 2F).
evidence: Supported by head entry measurements during Pavlovian conditioning.

claim: Robo2 mutant mice do not differ from control mice in pre-pulse inhibition of the acoustic startle reflex.
source: Robo2 mutant mice did not differ from control mice in PPI, and although they are hyperactive at baseline, they do not show increased sensitivity to MK-801. (Figure 4—figure supplement 2G–H).
evidence: Supported by pre-pulse inhibition measurements.

claim: Robo2 mutant mice do not show increased sensitivity to the psychomimetic NMDA receptor antagonist MK-801.
source: Robo2 mutant mice did not differ from control mice in PPI, and although they are hyperactive at baseline, they do not show increased sensitivity to MK-801. (Figure 4—figure supplement 2G–H).
evidence: Supported by locomotor activity measurements following MK-801 injection.

claim: Treatment of adult Slc6A3-iCre/ERT2::Robo2lox/lox mice with tamoxifen results in Cre-mediated recombination in dopamine neurons of the VTA and SNc.
source: Treatment of adult mice with the estrogen receptor agonist tamoxifen (75 mg/kg x 5 days) resulted in Cre-mediated recombination in dopamine neurons of the VTA and SNc (Figure 5A).
evidence: Supported by histological analysis showing tdTomato reporter expression in dopamine neurons.

claim: Tamoxifen-treated Slc6A3-iCre/ERT2::Robo2lox/lox mice do not show hyperactivity relative to sham-injected controls.
source: Behavioral analysis of tamoxifen treated DAT-iCreER::Robo2lox/lox mice did not result in hyperactivity, altered psychostimulant response to cocaine, or learning deficits relative to sham injected Slc6A3-iCre/ERT2::Robo2lox/lox mice (Figure 5B–C; Figure 5—figure supplement 1A–D).
evidence: Supported by locomotor activity measurements across the day-night cycle.

claim: Tamoxifen-treated Slc6A3-iCre/ERT2::Robo2lox/lox mice do not show altered psychostimulant response to cocaine relative to sham-injected controls.
source: Behavioral analysis of tamoxifen treated DAT-iCreER::Robo2lox/lox mice did not result in hyperactivity, altered psychostimulant response to cocaine, or learning deficits relative to sham injected Slc6A3-iCre/ERT2::Robo2lox/lox mice (Figure 5B–C; Figure 5—figure supplement 1A–D).
evidence: Supported by locomotor activity measurements following cocaine injection.

claim: Tamoxifen-treated Slc6A3-iCre/ERT2::Robo2lox/lox mice do not show learning deficits relative to sham-injected controls.
source: Behavioral analysis of tamoxifen treated DAT-iCreER::Robo2lox/lox mice did not result in hyperactivity, altered psychostimulant response to cocaine, or learning deficits relative to sham injected Slc6A3-iCre/ERT2::Robo2lox/lox mice (Figure 5B–C; Figure 5—figure supplement 1A–D).
evidence: Supported by Pavlovian conditioning behavioral data.

claim: Slc6A3-Cre::Robo2∆/lox mice do not show hyperactivity relative to control mice.
source: Similar to Slc6A3-iCre/ERT2::Robo2lox/lox mice, Slc6A3-Cre::Robo2∆/lox mice did not show hyperactivity, altered psychostimulant response to cocaine, or learning deficits relative to control mice (DAT-iCreER::Robo2∆/+) (Figure 5E–F; Figure 5—figure supplement 1F–I).
evidence: Supported by locomotor activity measurements across the day-night cycle.

claim: Slc6A3-Cre::Robo2∆/lox mice do not show altered psychostimulant response to cocaine relative to control mice.
source: Similar to Slc6A3-iCre/ERT2::Robo2lox/lox mice, Slc6A3-Cre::Robo2∆/lox mice did not show hyperactivity, altered psychostimulant response to cocaine, or learning deficits relative to control mice (DAT-iCreER::Robo2∆/+) (Figure 5E–F; Figure 5—figure supplement 1F–I).
evidence: Supported by locomotor activity measurements following cocaine injection.

claim: Slc6A3-Cre::Robo2∆/lox mice do not show learning deficits relative to control mice.
source: Similar to Slc6A3-iCre/ERT2::Robo2lox/lox mice, Slc6A3-Cre::Robo2∆/lox mice did not show hyperactivity, altered psychostimulant response to cocaine, or learning deficits relative to control mice (DAT-iCreER::Robo2∆/+) (Figure 5E–F; Figure 5—figure supplement 1F–I).
evidence: Supported by Pavlovian conditioning behavioral data.

claim: Ribotag analysis following injection of AAV1-FLEX-Rpl22HA into Slc6A3-Cre::Robo2∆/lox mice demonstrates a significant reduction in Robo2 mRNA in dopamine neurons.
source: Consistent with inactivation of Robo2, Ribotag analysis following injection of an AAV containing Cre-dependent Rpl22HA (AAV1-FLEX-Rpl22HA) demonstrated a significant reduction in Robo2 mRNA in dopamine neurons (Figure 5—figure supplement 1E); consistent with nonsense-mediated mRNA decay (Gibson et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by Ribotag immunoprecipitation and qRT-PCR data.

claim: AAV1-Cre-GFP::Slc6A3-Cre::Robo2∆/lox mice are hyperactive compared to controls.
source: Similar to injection of AAV1-Cre-GFP into the VTA of Robo2lox/lox mice, AAV1-Cre-GFP::Slc6A3-Cre::Robo2∆/lox mice were hyperactive, had inverted cocaine responses, and deficits in Pavlovian associative learning (Figure 5H–L; Figure 5—figure supplement 1J–K).
evidence: Supported by locomotor activity measurements across the day-night cycle.

claim: AAV1-Cre-GFP::Slc6A3-Cre::Robo2∆/lox mice have inverted cocaine responses compared to controls.
source: Similar to injection of AAV1-Cre-GFP into the VTA of Robo2lox/lox mice, AAV1-Cre-GFP::Slc6A3-Cre::Robo2∆/lox mice were hyperactive, had inverted cocaine responses, and deficits in Pavlovian associative learning (Figure 5H–L; Figure 5—figure supplement 1J–K).
evidence: Supported by locomotor activity measurements following cocaine injection.

claim: AAV1-Cre-GFP::Slc6A3-Cre::Robo2∆/lox mice have deficits in Pavlovian associative learning compared to controls.
source: Similar to injection of AAV1-Cre-GFP into the VTA of Robo2lox/lox mice, AAV1-Cre-GFP::Slc6A3-Cre::Robo2∆/lox mice were hyperactive, had inverted cocaine responses, and deficits in Pavlovian associative learning (Figure 5H–L; Figure 5—figure supplement 1J–K).
evidence: Supported by Pavlovian conditioning behavioral data.

claim: Robo2 inactivation is required in non-dopamine producing neurons to induce the observed behavioral phenotypes.
source: These results indicate that Robo2 inactivation is required in non-dopamine producing neurons to induce the observed behavioral phenotypes.
evidence: Inference based on the lack of phenotypes in dopamine-specific Robo2 knockout mice and the presence of phenotypes when both dopamine and non-dopamine neurons are targeted.

claim: Inactivation of GABAergic transmission in the VTA of Slc6a32A1-Cre::AAV1-FLEX-GFP-TetX mice results in rapid weight loss and compromised health in a number of animals.
source: Unexpectedly, inactivation of GABAergic transmission in the VTA of Slc6a32A1-Cre::AAV1-FLEX-GFP-TetX mice resulted in rapid weight loss and compromised health in a number of animals (11 out of 20 fell below 80% of their pre-surgery bodyweight and were removed from the study) that could not be further assessed for behavioral changes.
evidence: Observation of weight loss and compromised health in experimental animals.

claim: Slc6a32A1-Cre::AAV1-FLEX-GFP-TetX mice that did not show dramatic weight loss show hyperactivity compared to controls.
source: Of the remaining Slc6a32A1-Cre::AAV1-FLEX-GFP-TetX mice (9 out of 20) that did not show dramatic weight loss, possibly due to a reduced efficiency of GABA inactivation, we observed hyperactivity and inverted locomotor responses to cocaine (Figure 6B–E).
evidence: Supported by locomotor activity measurements across the day-night cycle.

claim: Slc6a32A1-Cre::AAV1-FLEX-GFP-TetX mice that did not show dramatic weight loss show inverted locomotor responses to cocaine compared to controls.
source: Of the remaining Slc6a32A1-Cre::AAV1-FLEX-GFP-TetX mice (9 out of 20) that did not show dramatic weight loss, possibly due to a reduced efficiency of GABA inactivation, we observed hyperactivity and inverted locomotor responses to cocaine (Figure 6B–E).
evidence: Supported by locomotor activity measurements following cocaine injection.

claim: Reduced GABAergic control of the VTA following Robo2 inactivation is likely the cause of hyperactivity and altered behavioral responses to psychostimulants.
source: These findings suggest that reduced GABAergic control of the VTA following Robo2 inactivation is likely the cause of hyperactivity and altered behavioral responses to psychostimulants.
evidence: Inference based on the phenocopy of Robo2 mutant phenotypes by selective inactivation of GABAergic transmission in the VTA.

claim: Robo2 is critical for the maintenance of inhibitory synapses in the adult ventral tegmental area.
source: Here we find that the developmental axon guidance receptor Roundabout 2 (Robo2) is critical for the maintenance of inhibitory synapses in the adult ventral tegmental area (VTA), a brain region important for the production of the neurotransmitter dopamine.
evidence: Supported by electrophysiological data showing reduced sIPSC frequency following Robo2 inactivation.

claim: Following selective genetic inactivation of Robo2 in the adult VTA of mice, reduced inhibitory control results in altered neural activity patterns.
source: Following selective genetic inactivation of Robo2 in the adult VTA of mice, reduced inhibitory control results in altered neural activity patterns, enhanced phasic dopamine release, behavioral hyperactivity, associative learning deficits, and a paradoxical inversion of psychostimulant responses.
evidence: Supported by in vivo electrophysiology data showing increased burst duration and spikes per burst.

claim: Following selective genetic inactivation of Robo2 in the adult VTA of mice, reduced inhibitory control results in enhanced phasic dopamine release.
source: Following selective genetic inactivation of Robo2 in the adult VTA of mice, reduced inhibitory control results in altered neural activity patterns, enhanced phasic dopamine release, behavioral hyperactivity, associative learning deficits, and a paradoxical inversion of psychostimulant responses.
evidence: Supported by fast scan cyclic voltammetry data showing elevated dopamine release at lower stimulus intensities.

claim: Following selective genetic inactivation of Robo2 in the adult VTA of mice, reduced inhibitory control results in behavioral hyperactivity.
source: Following selective genetic inactivation of Robo2 in the adult VTA of mice, reduced inhibitory control results in altered neural activity patterns, enhanced phasic dopamine release, behavioral hyperactivity, associative learning deficits, and a paradoxical inversion of psychostimulant responses.
evidence: Supported by locomotor activity measurements showing increased activity in mutant mice.

claim: Following selective genetic inactivation of Robo2 in the adult VTA of mice, reduced inhibitory control results in associative learning deficits.
source: Following selective genetic inactivation of Robo2 in the adult VTA of mice, reduced inhibitory control results in altered neural activity patterns, enhanced phasic dopamine release, behavioral hyperactivity, associative learning deficits, and a paradoxical inversion of psychostimulant responses.
evidence: Supported by Pavlovian conditioning data showing impaired discrimination between predictive and non-predictive cues.

claim: Following selective genetic inactivation of Robo2 in the adult VTA of mice, reduced inhibitory control results in a paradoxical inversion of psychostimulant responses.
source: Following selective genetic inactivation of Robo2 in the adult VTA of mice, reduced inhibitory control results in altered neural activity patterns, enhanced phasic dopamine release, behavioral hyperactivity, associative learning deficits, and a paradoxical inversion of psychostimulant responses.
evidence: Supported by locomotor activity measurements showing decreased activity in response to cocaine and amphetamine in mutant mice.

claim: The behavioral phenotypes following Robo2 inactivation in the adult VTA could be phenocopied by selective inactivation of synaptic transmission from local GABAergic neurons of the VTA.
source: These behavioral phenotypes could be phenocopied by selective inactivation of synaptic transmission from local GABAergic neurons of the VTA, demonstrating an important function for Robo2 in regulating the excitatory and inhibitory balance of the adult brain.
evidence: Supported by behavioral data from Slc6a32A1-Cre::AAV1-FLEX-GFP-TetX mice showing hyperactivity and inverted cocaine responses.

claim: Robo2 has an important function in regulating the excitatory and inhibitory balance of the adult brain.
source: These behavioral phenotypes could be phenocopied by selective inactivation of synaptic transmission from local GABAergic neurons of the VTA, demonstrating an important function for Robo2 in regulating the excitatory and inhibitory balance of the adult brain.
evidence: Inference based on the phenocopy of Robo2 mutant phenotypes by selective inactivation of GABAergic transmission in the VTA.

claim: The midbrain dopamine system, consisting of the VTA and substantia nigra pars compacta (SNc), is essential for motor function, motivation, reward, learning, and memory.
source: The midbrain dopamine system, consisting of the VTA and substantia nigra pars compacta (SNc), is essential for motor function, motivation, reward, learning, and memory.
evidence: Draws from established scientific consensus about the function of the midbrain dopamine system.

claim: Alterations in the activity patterns of dopamine neurons have been proposed as a key contributor to mental illness.
source: Alterations in the activity patterns of dopamine neurons have been proposed as a key contributor to mental illness (Grace, 1991).
evidence: Supported by citation to Grace, 1991.

claim: Shifts in excitatory and inhibitory balance are increasingly linked to a variety of mental disorders including schizophrenia and autism.
source: In addition to dopamine, accumulating evidence points to an essential balance of excitatory and inhibitory neurotransmitter systems in the brain to allow for proper function. Shifts in this balance are increasingly linked to a variety of mental disorders including schizophrenia (Eichler and Meier, 2008) and autism (Nelson and Valakh, 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to Eichler and Meier, 2008 and Nelson and Valakh, 2015.

claim: Changes in inhibitory and excitatory strength in the VTA are proposed to underlie drug-seeking behavior.
source: The VTA dopamine system is also broadly implicated in addiction where changes in inhibitory and excitatory strength are proposed to underlie drug-seeking behavior (Chen et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citation to Chen et al., 2010.

claim: Robo2 was first discovered as one of the four mammalian homologs to the Drosophila Roundabout gene (Robo).
source: Robo2 was first discovered as one of the four mammalian homologs to the Drosophila Roundabout gene (Robo), which was named because of the unique axonal recrossing pattern generated at the CNS midline (Seeger et al., 1993; Kidd et al., 1998; Brose et al., 1999; Simpson et al., 2000).
evidence: Supported by citations to Seeger et al., 1993; Kidd et al., 1998; Brose et al., 1999; Simpson et al., 2000.

claim: Robo family members perform additional axon guidance functions to regulate brain wiring broadly throughout the nervous system.
source: Further studies found that Robo family members perform additional axon guidance functions to regulate brain wiring broadly throughout the nervous system (Ypsilanti and Chedotal, 2014), including midbrain dopamine neurons (Dugan et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citations to Ypsilanti and Chedotal, 2014 and Dugan et al., 2011.

claim: Robo2 functions include cell migration, synaptogenesis, synaptic plasticity, neuronal survival, and dendritic patterning during prenatal and early postnatal development.
source: Additional studies expanded the essential functions of Robo2 to include cell migration, synaptogenesis, synaptic plasticity, neuronal survival, and dendritic patterning during prenatal and early postnatal development (Shen and Cowan, 2010; Gibson et al., 2014; Koropouli and Kolodkin, 2014; Ypsilanti and Chedotal, 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to Shen and Cowan, 2010; Gibson et al., 2014; Koropouli and Kolodkin, 2014; Ypsilanti and Chedotal, 2014.

claim: The neuronal axon guidance receptor deleted in colorectal cancer (DCC) is highly expressed in the adult dopamine neurons.
source: Previous studies demonstrate that the neuronal axon guidance receptor deleted in colorectal cancer (DCC) is also highly expressed in the adult dopamine neurons, is dynamically regulated by amphetamine (Yetnikoff et al., 2007), and mice with haploinsufficiency for DCC demonstrate blunted responses to the psychomotor activating effects of amphetamine (Flores et al., 2005).
evidence: Supported by citations to Yetnikoff et al., 2007 and Flores et al., 2005.

claim: DCC is dynamically regulated by amphetamine.
source: Previous studies demonstrate that the neuronal axon guidance receptor deleted in colorectal cancer (DCC) is also highly expressed in the adult dopamine neurons, is dynamically regulated by amphetamine (Yetnikoff et al., 2007), and mice with haploinsufficiency for DCC demonstrate blunted responses to the psychomotor activating effects of amphetamine (Flores et al., 2005).
evidence: Supported by citation to Yetnikoff et al., 2007.

claim: Mice with haploinsufficiency for DCC demonstrate blunted responses to the psychomotor activating effects of amphetamine.
source: Previous studies demonstrate that the neuronal axon guidance receptor deleted in colorectal cancer (DCC) is also highly expressed in the adult dopamine neurons, is dynamically regulated by amphetamine (Yetnikoff et al., 2007), and mice with haploinsufficiency for DCC demonstrate blunted responses to the psychomotor activating effects of amphetamine (Flores et al., 2005).
evidence: Supported by citation to Flores et al., 2005.

claim: DCC regulates excitatory synaptic transmission in the adult hippocampus.
source: Consistent with the continued function of DCC in the adult nervous system, it has recently been demonstrated that DCC regulates excitatory synaptic transmission in the adult hippocampus (Horn et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to Horn et al., 2013.

claim: During early development of the spinal cord, Robo and DCC signaling have opposing roles in commissural axon guidance.
source: During early development of the spinal cord, Robo and DCC signaling have opposing roles in commissural axon guidance, with DCC activation promoting axon growth toward the midline and Robo serving as a chemorepellant to prevent recrossing (Tessier-Lavigne and Goodman, 1996).
evidence: Supported by citation to Tessier-Lavigne and Goodman, 1996.

claim: DCC activation promotes axon growth toward the midline during early development of the spinal cord.
source: During early development of the spinal cord, Robo and DCC signaling have opposing roles in commissural axon guidance, with DCC activation promoting axon growth toward the midline and Robo serving as a chemorepellant to prevent recrossing (Tessier-Lavigne and Goodman, 1996).
evidence: Supported by citation to Tessier-Lavigne and Goodman, 1996.

claim: Robo serves as a chemorepellant to prevent recrossing during early development of the spinal cord.
source: During early development of the spinal cord, Robo and DCC signaling have opposing roles in commissural axon guidance, with DCC activation promoting axon growth toward the midline and Robo serving as a chemorepellant to prevent recrossing (Tessier-Lavigne and Goodman, 1996).
evidence: Supported by citation to Tessier-Lavigne and Goodman, 1996.

claim: Robo receptors are activated upon binding chemorepellants of the Slit family, Slit1, Slit2, and Slit3.
source: Robo receptors are activated upon binding chemorepellants of the Slit family, Slit1, Slit2, and Slit3 (Tessier-Lavigne and Goodman, 1996), which cause growth cone collapse through cytoskeletal remodeling via Rho-family GTPase signaling (Wong et al., 2001).
evidence: Supported by citation to Tessier-Lavigne and Goodman, 1996.

claim: Slit ligands cause growth cone collapse through cytoskeletal remodeling via Rho-family GTPase signaling.
source: Robo receptors are activated upon binding chemorepellants of the Slit family, Slit1, Slit2, and Slit3 (Tessier-Lavigne and Goodman, 1996), which cause growth cone collapse through cytoskeletal remodeling via Rho-family GTPase signaling (Wong et al., 2001).
evidence: Supported by citation to Wong et al., 2001.

claim: All three genes for the Slit ligands and the receptors Robo1 and Robo2 are expressed in the adult midbrain, including the VTA and SNc.
source: All three genes for the Slit ligands and the receptors Robo1 and Robo2 (Marillat et al., 2002) are expressed in the adult midbrain, including the VTA and SNc
evidence: Supported by citation to Marillat et al., 2002.

claim: Genes involved in Robo signaling have been linked to schizophrenia, autism, conduct disorder, intellectual disability, language impairment, and bipolar depression.
source: Of further interest, genes involved in Robo signaling have been linked to schizophrenia, autism, conduct disorder, intellectual disability, language impairment, and bipolar depression (Anitha et al., 2008; Potkin et al., 2009, 2010; Viding et al., 2010; Suda et al., 2011; Dadds et al., 2013; St Pourcain et al., 2014; Wang et al., 2014; Okbay et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to Anitha et al., 2008; Potkin et al., 2009, 2010; Viding et al., 2010; Suda et al., 2011; Dadds et al., 2013; St Pourcain et al., 2014; Wang et al., 2014; Okbay et al., 2016.

claim: The observed behavioral phenotype of inverted psychostimulant responses is a rare genetic finding.
source: The observed behavioral phenotype of inverted psychostimulant responses is a rare genetic finding. Numerous other genetic models have been described that cause hyperactivity, but few have inverted psychostimulant responses (Leo and Gainetdinov, 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to Leo and Gainetdinov, 2013.

claim: Numerous other genetic models have been described that cause hyperactivity, but few have inverted psychostimulant responses.
source: The observed behavioral phenotype of inverted psychostimulant responses is a rare genetic finding. Numerous other genetic models have been described that cause hyperactivity, but few have inverted psychostimulant responses (Leo and Gainetdinov, 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to Leo and Gainetdinov, 2013.

claim: Similar to inactivation of the dopamine transporter, Robo2 mutant mice show increased sensitivity to the serotonin transport blocker fluoxetine.
source: Similar to inactivation of the dopamine transporter (Gainetdinov et al., 1999), we observed increased sensitivity to the serotonin transport blocker fluoxetine, suggesting the hyperactivity associated with loss of Robo2 is due to a potential enhancement of the serotonin system.
evidence: Supported by citation to Gainetdinov et al., 1999 and data showing increased sensitivity to fluoxetine.

claim: The hyperactivity associated with loss of Robo2 is due to a potential enhancement of the serotonin system.
source: Similar to inactivation of the dopamine transporter (Gainetdinov et al., 1999), we observed increased sensitivity to the serotonin transport blocker fluoxetine, suggesting the hyperactivity associated with loss of Robo2 is due to a potential enhancement of the serotonin system.
evidence: Speculation based on the observed increased sensitivity to fluoxetine.

claim: Robo receptors interact with A-kinase anchoring proteins (AKAPs).
source: It was recently shown that Robo receptors interact with A-kinase anchoring proteins (AKAPs) (Samelson et al., 2015), placing Robo receptors in key scaffolding complexes.
evidence: Supported by citation to Samelson et al., 2015.

claim: AKAP 79/150 is expressed in dopamine and non-dopamine neurons in the VTA where it regulates GABAergic synaptic transmission.
source: It has also been shown that AKAP 79/150 is expressed in dopamine and non-dopamine neurons in the VTA where it regulates GABAergic synaptic transmission. Intriguingly, disruption of AKAP function induces a long-term depression like effect on GABAergic synapse (Dacher et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to Dacher et al., 2013.

claim: Disruption of AKAP function induces a long-term depression like effect on GABAergic synapse.
source: It has also been shown that AKAP 79/150 is expressed in dopamine and non-dopamine neurons in the VTA where it regulates GABAergic synaptic transmission. Intriguingly, disruption of AKAP function induces a long-term depression like effect on GABAergic synapse (Dacher et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to Dacher et al., 2013.

claim: An intriguing possibility is that Robo2 receptors interact with AKAPs to stabilize inhibitory synaptic connectivity.
source: Thus, an intriguing possibility is that Robo2 receptors interact with AKAPs to stabilize inhibitory synaptic connectivity.
evidence: Speculation based on the known interaction between Robo receptors and AKAPs and the role of AKAPs in regulating GABAergic synaptic transmission.

claim: In Drosophila, during commissural axon pathfinding, Robo2 interacts with Robo1 in trans to suppress the repulsive properties of Robo1.
source: Both Robo1 and Robo2 are expressed in the VTA, and it has been demonstrated in Drosophila that during commissural axon pathfinding, Robo2 interacts with Robo1 in trans to suppress the repulsive properties of Robo1 (Evans et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to Evans et al., 2015.

claim: During cocaine sensitization, changes in spine density in the striatum results from inhibition of the small Rho-family GTPase, Rac1.
source: Interestingly, during cocaine sensitization, changes in spine density in the striatum results from inhibition of the small Rho-family GTPase, Rac1, which is a known effector molecule for Robo signaling, and is a potent regulator of spine turnover during development (Dietz et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation to Dietz et al., 2012.

claim: Rac1 is a known effector molecule for Robo signaling.
source: Interestingly, during cocaine sensitization, changes in spine density in the striatum results from inhibition of the small Rho-family GTPase, Rac1, which is a known effector molecule for Robo signaling, and is a potent regulator of spine turnover during development (Dietz et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation to Dietz et al., 2012.

claim: Rac1 is a potent regulator of spine turnover during development.
source: Interestingly, during cocaine sensitization, changes in spine density in the striatum results from inhibition of the small Rho-family GTPase, Rac1, which is a known effector molecule for Robo signaling, and is a potent regulator of spine turnover during development (Dietz et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation to Dietz et al., 2012.

claim: Cocaine sensitization reduces inhibitory synaptic transmission in the VTA.
source: In addition, cocaine sensitization reduces inhibitory synaptic transmission in the VTA (Liu et al., 2005) that may be mediated in part by Robo2 signaling.
evidence: Supported by citation to Liu et al., 2005.

claim: Cocaine sensitization-induced reduction in inhibitory synaptic transmission in the VTA may be mediated in part by Robo2 signaling.
source: In addition, cocaine sensitization reduces inhibitory synaptic transmission in the VTA (Liu et al., 2005) that may be mediated in part by Robo2 signaling.
evidence: Speculation based on the observed role of Robo2 in regulating inhibitory synaptic transmission.

claim: The Robo2lox/lox mouse line was generated as described previously.
source: The Robo2lox/lox mouse line was generated as described (Lu et al., 2007).
evidence: Supported by citation to Lu et al., 2007.

claim: In the Robo2lox/lox mouse line, loxP recognition sites are inserted to flank exon 5 of Robo2, and following Cre-mediated recombination, a frameshift occurs resulting in a premature stop codon in exon 6.
source: In this line, loxP recognition sites are inserted to flank exon 5 of Robo2, and following Cre-mediated recombination, a frameshift occurs resulting in a premature stop codon in exon 6 (Figure 1B).
evidence: Description of the genetic modification in the Robo2lox/lox mouse line.

claim: Putative dopamine neurons in an acute slice preparation were identified by the presence of an afterhyperpolarization induced current (Ih).
source: Putative dopamine neurons in an acute slice preparation from AAV1-Cre-GFP::Robo2lox/lox (mutant) and AAV1-∆Cre-GFP::Robo2lox/lox (control) were identified by the presence of an afterhyperpolarization induced current (Ih) as described (Johnson and North, 1992) (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A), though this is not a definitive feature of all dopamine producing neurons (Margolis et al., 2006).
evidence: Supported by citations to Johnson and North, 1992 and Margolis et al., 2006.

claim: The presence of an Ih current is not a definitive feature of all dopamine producing neurons.
source: Putative dopamine neurons in an acute slice preparation from AAV1-Cre-GFP::Robo2lox/lox (mutant) and AAV1-∆Cre-GFP::Robo2lox/lox (control) were identified by the presence of an afterhyperpolarization induced current (Ih) as described (Johnson and North, 1992) (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A), though this is not a definitive feature of all dopamine producing neurons (Margolis et al., 2006).
evidence: Supported by citation to Margolis et al., 2006.

claim: GABAergic synaptic transmission potently regulates dopamine neuron activity patterns.
source: GABAergic synaptic transmission potently regulates dopamine neuron activity patterns (Paladini and Tepper, 1999).
evidence: Supported by citation to Paladini and Tepper, 1999.

claim: The Slc6A3-Cre mouse line has been previously shown to effectively inactivate genes in virtually all dopamine producing neurons.
source: The conventional Cre-driver mouse line (Slc6A3-Cre) has been previously shown to effectively inactivate genes in virtually all dopamine producing neurons (Engblom et al., 2008; Zweifel et al., 2008).
evidence: Supported by citations to Engblom et al., 2008 and Zweifel et al., 2008.

claim: One caveat to the Slc6A3-Cre mouse line is that the early expression of Cre may result in developmental compensations.
source: One caveat to this mouse line is that the early expression of Cre may result in developmental compensations (Engblom et al., 2008).
evidence: Supported by citation to Engblom et al., 2008.

claim: The reduction in Robo2 mRNA in dopamine neurons following Cre-mediated recombination is consistent with nonsense-mediated mRNA decay.
source: Consistent with inactivation of Robo2, Ribotag analysis following injection of an AAV containing Cre-dependent Rpl22HA (AAV1-FLEX-Rpl22HA) demonstrated a significant reduction in Robo2 mRNA in dopamine neurons (Figure 5—figure supplement 1E); consistent with nonsense-mediated mRNA decay (Gibson et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to Gibson et al., 2014.

claim: Robo2 signaling strongly implicates balanced excitatory and inhibitory control of the midbrain as a likely source of ADHD-like phenotypes.
source: Given the link between hyperactivity and paradoxical calming by psychostimulants in ADHD, it is attractive to think that Robo2 regulation of inhibitory control of the midbrain may play an important role in this disorder. Although selective inactivation of Robo2 exclusively in the adult VTA is not a true genetic model of ADHD, our results strongly implicate balanced excitatory and inhibitory control of the midbrain as a likely source of ADHD-like phenotypes.
evidence: Inference based on the observed hyperactivity and inverted psychostimulant responses in Robo2 mutant mice.

claim: Drugs targeting specific GABAA receptors in the VTA may be a promising therapeutic avenue for multiple disorders.
source: Given the high degree of specificity for partial GABA agonists in targeting GABA receptors with specific subunit compositions (Hoestgaard-Jensen et al., 2014), drugs targeting specific GABAA receptors in the VTA may be a promising therapeutic avenue for multiple disorders.
evidence: Speculation based on the observed role of GABAergic transmission in the VTA and the specificity of partial GABA agonists.

claim: An intriguing possibility is that Robo2 receptors interact with Robo1 either in cis or in trans to stabilize synapses.
source: Another, non-mutually exclusive possibility is that Robo2 interacts with Robo1 either in cis or in trans to stabilize synapses.
evidence: Speculation based on the known interaction between Robo2 and Robo1 in Drosophila.
